d.title: Timeless Timing Attacks: Exploiting Concurrency to Leak Secrets over Remote Connections
d.summary: Concurrency-based timing attacks compare the order in which two simultaneous requests return rather than their absolute times, so network jitter cancels out. Sent as multiplexed HTTP/2 requests inside one packet, or over Tor, they resolve remote execution differences of about 100 nanoseconds, and are demonstrated against web servers, onion services and EAP-pwd.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: The single-packet attack: making remote race-conditions 'local'
d.summary: Explains how network jitter affects remote race-condition testing and examines the protocol requirements for synchronized requests. The article compares HTTP, WebSocket and SMTP behavior, distinguishing demonstrated HTTP/2 results from proposals that still require experimental validation.
d.context: Analyzes protocol applicability and separates proposed adaptations from proven results.

d.title: How to build custom scanners for web security research automation

d.title: Forgot password? Taking over user accounts Kaminsky style
d.summary: Registering accounts on 146 real web applications with per-target subdomain e-mail addresses, then proxying the resulting MX lookups, to measure which applications still meet the preconditions for Kaminsky-style cache poisoning or IP-fragmentation attacks. Poisoning such a resolver redirects password-reset mail to the attacker and takes over accounts.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: Melting the DNS Iceberg: Taking over your infrastructure Kaminsky style
d.summary: A survey of closed, non-publicly-reachable DNS resolvers, reached indirectly by sending mail that forces a target mail server to query an attacker-controlled authoritative nameserver for SPF, DKIM and DMARC records. Resolvers found without source port randomisation are poisonable by a classic Kaminsky attack, enabling MX redirection, password-reset interception and account takeover.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

Exploiting ASP.NET TemplateParser — Part I: Sitecore (CVE-2023-35813)
Exploiting ASP.NET TemplateParser — Part II: SharePoint (CVE-2023-33160)
d.summary: A null byte appended to the Namespace attribute of an ASP.NET @ Register directive truncates type-name resolution, letting an attacker instantiate an arbitrary generic type whose type argument dictates a property type and so which TypeConverter or Parse method runs. On SharePoint this defeated the Safe Controls allowlist and gave remote code execution on-premises and online.

d.title: A Security Review of SharePoint Site Pages
d.summary: SharePoint parses customised site pages with CompilationMode.Never so inline code never runs, but where an administrator allows compilation with server-side script still disabled, the namespace value of an import or register directive is copied verbatim into the generated C# and can be closed and reopened to define a class. That yields code execution on the server.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: Room for Escape: Scribbling Outside the Lines of Template Security
d.summary: Templates that untrusted users may edit break out of their sandboxes: SharePoint's safe-mode page parser is fooled by delayed data binding into parsing a user site page as a trusted application page, and Java engines such as FreeMarker, Velocity and Jinjava are escaped through objects left reachable in the template context. The result is remote code execution as an unprivileged CMS user.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.
